# (APPENDIX) Appendix {-}

# Course Labs: Walkthroughs {#course-labs}

The course *Generative AI with Large Language Models* (DeepLearning.AI / AWS,
Coursera) had three hands-on labs. All three used one task: summarizing
dialogues with Flan-T5. Each lab applied one stage of the lifecycle
(Section \@ref(generative-ai-project-lifecycle)) to that task: prompting,
then fine-tuning, then alignment.

This appendix records what each lab did and what it teaches. It is written in
my own words, and the course notebooks are not reproduced.

> **About the numbers.** Results below are **as reported in the course labs,
> not reproduced** here. They came from small samples and short training runs
> on 2023-era library versions. Read them as directional evidence. The
> libraries used (Hugging Face `transformers`, `peft`, `trl`, and `evaluate`)
> have changed their APIs since then, so check current documentation before
> rebuilding any of these workflows.

## Common setup

| Item | Choice |
|:-----|:-------|
| Model | `google/flan-t5-base`: an instruction-tuned encoder–decoder model of about 250M parameters (Chapter \@ref(instruction-fine-tuning-and-evaluation)) |
| Data | **DialogSum** [@chen2021dialogsum]: about 13,000 everyday and service dialogues, each with a human-written summary. Not part of Flan-T5's training mixture. |
| Task | Generate a one- or two-sentence summary of a dialogue |
| Reference | The human summary, used for side-by-side reading and as the ROUGE reference |
| Limits | Flan-T5's 512-token input limit; long dialogues get truncated |

## Lab 1: Summarization with prompting and generation settings

**Goal.** Find out how far prompting alone can take a small model, before any
training. This is the first step with any new model and dataset.

**Steps:**

1. **No instruction.** Pass the raw dialogue to the model. The output was a
   continuation or fragment, not a summary. The model could not tell what task
   was wanted.
2. **Zero-shot instruction.** Wrap the dialogue as "Summarize the following
   conversation. … Summary:". The output became summary-like but missed
   nuance.
3. **Model-native template.** Use one of the phrasings from Flan-T5's own
   training templates ("Dialogue: … What was going on?"). This gave a modest
   improvement. Prompts that match the model's instruction-tuning format
   tend to work better.
4. **One-shot and few-shot.** Prepend one, then three, complete examples
   (dialogue plus human summary) before the target dialogue. One-shot helped;
   few-shot did not clearly beat one-shot on the example shown. Some few-shot
   prompts also exceeded the 512-token limit.
5. **Generation settings.** Vary `max_new_tokens`, sampling on or off, and
   temperature (Section \@ref(configuring-generative-ai-models)). Low
   temperature gave conservative, repeatable summaries. High temperature gave
   varied and sometimes incoherent ones.

**Lessons:**

- With a small model, the instruction wording and format matter, and
  in-context examples give a limited lift. The course team's rule of thumb was
  that more than five or six examples rarely help.
- Examples consume the context window. For a 512-token model this is a hard
  constraint.
- When prompting plateaus below the quality you need, fine-tune (Lab 2).

## Lab 2: Full fine-tuning vs. LoRA

**Goal.** Improve zero-shot summarization by fine-tuning on DialogSum, and
compare full fine-tuning with parameter-efficient LoRA (Section \@ref(peft)).

**Steps:**

1. **Format the data as instructions.** Map each record to the prompt
   "Summarize the following conversation. {dialogue} Summary:", with the human
   summary as the target. Tokenize, and split into training, validation, and
   test sets.
2. **Full instruction fine-tuning.** Train all ~250M parameters with the
   Hugging Face `Trainer`. The in-lab run used a small subsample and very few
   steps to save time. A checkpoint trained longer offline was then loaded
   for evaluation. That checkpoint was about **945 MB**, a full copy of the
   model.
3. **LoRA fine-tuning.** Wrap the same base model with a LoRA configuration of
   rank $r = 32$, a relatively high rank. That left about **1.4% of
   parameters trainable**. Train the same way, then load an offline-trained
   adapter of about **14 MB**.
4. **Inference.** Load the adapter on top of the frozen base model with
   training disabled. That reported 0% trainable parameters and avoids
   allocating training state.
5. **Evaluate.** Compare human, base-model, fully fine-tuned, and
   LoRA-tuned summaries, first by reading them and then with ROUGE
   (Section \@ref(evaluating-model-performance-in-language-tasks)) on a
   larger held-out set.

**Reported results:**

- Full fine-tuning clearly beat the base model on every ROUGE variant. The
  walkthrough quoted about **18** (ROUGE-1), **10** (ROUGE-2), **13**
  (ROUGE-L), and **13.7** (ROUGE-Lsum) "percent" higher. It did not say whether
  these are relative changes or absolute ROUGE points. The lecture summarized
  the same comparison as absolute ROUGE-1 gains of **+0.19** (full) and
  **+0.17** (LoRA), which suggests absolute points.
- LoRA scored about **1–2 points below** full fine-tuning across the ROUGE
  metrics. It trained about 1.4% of the parameters and stored about 14 MB
  instead of about 945 MB.

**Lessons:**

- A small amount of task-specific instruction data can lift a general instruct
  model substantially on a narrow task.
- LoRA gives up a little quality for large savings in training memory and
  storage. The base model can be shared, with one small adapter per task.
- Read outputs as well as metrics. A ROUGE gain says nothing directly about
  invented details or missing actions.

## Lab 3: Detoxifying with RLHF (PPO)

**Goal.** Make the Lab 2 summarizer less likely to produce hateful or toxic
language, using reinforcement learning against a reward model
(Chapter \@ref(alignment-human-feedback)).

**Components:**

| Role | What was used |
|:-----|:--------------|
| Policy | The LoRA-tuned Flan-T5 from Lab 2, plus a **value head**. The head is a single linear layer from the 768-dimensional hidden state to a scalar: 768 weights plus 1 bias. Only the LoRA adapter and the value head were trained. |
| Reference policy | A frozen copy of the Lab 2 model, used for the KL penalty |
| Reward model | An off-the-shelf RoBERTa hate-speech classifier with two classes, *not hate* and *hate*. The **logit of the "not hate" class** was the reward. |
| Algorithm | PPO from the `trl` library, with batch size 16 and few PPO epochs to keep the run short |
| Evaluation | Mean and standard deviation of the classifier's *hate* probability over generated summaries, before and after training |

**Steps:**

1. Build prompts from DialogSum dialogues, sampling input lengths to fit the
   model's context.
2. Measure the baseline toxicity of the Lab 2 model's summaries.
3. For each batch: generate summaries, score each (prompt, summary) pair with
   the classifier, and pass the prompts, responses, and rewards to a PPO step.
   The KL divergence to the reference model was monitored so that the policy
   could not drift into reward hacking.
4. Re-measure toxicity, and compare summaries and rewards before and after.

**Reported results.** After a short run, rewards rose on many examples and
mean toxicity fell "by a decent amount". The KL divergence stayed roughly
stable during training. The course noted that the effect was modest because
DialogSum is not a toxic dataset to begin with. Training longer, on more toxic
prompts, would show a larger difference.

**Lessons:**

- **Check the reward's class index.** The classifier put "not hate" at index
  0. Optimizing the wrong index would actively *increase* toxicity. Reward
  definitions deserve tests of their own.
- **A classifier is a narrow reward.** The policy is optimized towards
  whatever this one model measures, which is why the KL penalty and human
  review of samples matter (Section \@ref(reward-hacking)).
- **PEFT makes RLHF affordable.** Training only the adapter and the value head
  kept memory low. The reference policy could share the frozen base weights.

## What the three labs show together

| Lab | Lifecycle stage | Lever | What changes | Main cost |
|:----|:----------------|:------|:-------------|:----------|
| 1 | Adapt (prompting) | Instructions, examples, generation settings | Only the input | Context tokens; limited ceiling |
| 2 | Adapt (fine-tuning) | Supervised training, full or LoRA | Weights or adapter | Labelled data and compute |
| 3 | Align | PPO against a reward model, with a KL penalty | Adapter and value head | Reward design, run stability, evaluation |

The progression is the one recommended throughout this part of the book:
start with prompting, fine-tune when prompting plateaus, align when outputs
must follow preferences that labels alone do not capture, and evaluate at
every step.
